session_title: Opening Remarks
speaker: Daren Tang
affiliation: Director General, World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO)
text:
Distinguished Delegates, dear colleagues, dear friends, good morning and welcome to the first global forum on IP and AI. Let me start by thanking the Ambassador of Kazakhstan, Mr. Karad Torabayev for being our Chair over the next two days. While WIPO has dealt with IP and AI issues for the past few years, this is the first time that we are convening the global community to discuss critical issues across the whole spectrum of IP rights, patents, trademarks, designs, copyrights and many, many others. Over the next two days we will look widely across this fast moving landscape, grapple with difficult issues and put our heads together on a wide range of topics ranging from authorship and inventorship to AI training, human likeness and the impact of AI on the administration and governance of IP. But this morning I want to start somewhere else.
I want to start with us as human beings. Humankind has been innovating for as long as we have existed. Fire, tools, agriculture, the wheel, cities and eventually modern science and technology all came from our ability to observe the world around us, imagine something different and turn their imagination into reality. And we have been creating for just as long. Some of the oldest traces our ancestors left behind are not tools for survival but cave paintings of incredible beauty that still haunt us today and carvings of bone, stone and ivory, objects of beauty, instrumental music and markers of ritual.
But in 1474, the way that we innovated itself underwent a revolutionary innovation with the birth of Intellectual Property. In that year, the Republic of Venice adopted what is widely regarded as the world’s first patent statute. Venice was then one of the great commercial and technological powers of the world and its statute spoke explicitly about attracting people of unusual ingenuity and encouraging them to invent things that would be useful to the Republic of Venice. It offered inventors protection for ten years against others reproducing their inventions without permission. And in return, these inventions would be placed in a register that would be open for public inspection, turbo charging the spread of technical knowledge.
This was not done out of an abstract love for the concept of IP but Venice existed in fierce competition with other cities and powers. Technology, knowledge and highly skilled people were sources of economic and strategic advantage. Venice, therefore, needed a way to encourage talented people to come to invent, to disclose their inventions and ultimately to put those inventions to productive use. And from that, we can draw an insight that remains at heart of the IP system today. Human ingenuity has tremendous value but societies need institutions that enable that value to move from the mind of an inventor into community, economy and society.
IP stepped into this institutional role and became a transmitted force in the history of human innovation. Therefore, that innovative technological and strategic needs of society was what created the need for IP and that’s what remains at the heart of the IP system. That distinction matters enormously at this point, at this moment in history because if technology changes profoundly and if the way society creates, innovates and exchanges value changes a bit, then we cannot assume that the institutions we have inherited including the IP system will always remain perfectly adapted to the world in which it serves. This is where artificial intelligence enters the picture. AI is often described as another technological revolution but I am increasingly convinced that that description does not quite capture what is happening.
Humanity has, of course, invented extraordinary general purpose technologies before. Machines extended our physical strength. The printing press reproduced and spread knowledge exponentially. Electricity transformed our ability to produce and transport energy. Computers expanded our ability to calculate and process information and the Internet transformed communication, distribution, trade, connection and commerce.
But AI is doing something different. It is reaching into activities that we have historically associated the human mind itself, reasoning, analysis, synthesis and for an increasing number of people, even cognition, creation and invention. For an organization concerned with IP, that matters profoundly because AI is not simply transforming another industry. It is beginning to transform the processes from which Intellectual Property itself emerges, imagination, conception and expression. We already see AI helping scientists search chemical spaces that no human could explore manually.
We see it analyzing medical images, designing new materials, writing sophisticated computer code, generating content and tackling increasingly complex mathematical problems, seemingly providing solutions to some problems that eluded the best human minds for decades. At the same time, a creator can now discover that his or her voice, face or style has been reproduced synthetically at extraordinary fidelity. Content of all types, music, films, videos and others are being produced and distributed at rates which are overwhelming. WIPO’s description of this forum deliberately captures both sides of that reality. AI is expanding the possibilities for invention and creativity while raising fundamental questions about rights, ownership and responsibility.
This development is moving extremely quickly. For some time now, commentators have tried to grapple with the deeper question of whether a machine truly thinks, understands, feels, imagines or might one day even become conscious. Those questions matter, of course. But given that AI has consistently broken every single prediction of the speed of its speed of development and the day is, in fact, coming where AI can itself create AI autonomously, we must really begin to address the practical implications of this technology and what AI will mean for humanity. Will it help us to find treatments for diseases that have resisted generations of medical research?
Will it accelerate solutions in food, energy and climate technologies? Will it review new materials, new mathematics and perhaps even new insights into the fundamental laws of nature? I sincerely hope so. But we also have to confront other possibilities. What happens to work when machines can perform an ever large share of cognitive and physical tasks?
What happens to human creators and machines can reproduce their voices, styles and creative expressions at almost no marginal cost? What happens to invention when AI becomes not simply an instrument used by an inventor but an increasingly consequential participant in the inventive process? And ultimately, how do we preserve human agency, dignity and meaning in a world in which some of the attributes we have considered uniquely human increasingly have analogous or even equivalent machine counterparts? I confess that I first began preparing for today’s speech, my instinct was to make this rather safe, balanced, moderate, reassuring, UN style. But the more I thought about the scale and speed of what is happening, the less honest that seemed.
Because this may no longer be a moment for safe conversations, for wait and see, for business as usual. The decisions that governments, technology companies, creators, innovators and institutions take over just the next few years will shape the relationship between humanity and technology for generations to come. IP is, of course, only one part of that much larger story but it is an important part and for those of us gathered under this roof, it is our part. So I will propose three fundamental questions for us to confront as the global IP community. First, what should the IP system protect and incentivize in the age of AI?
The modern IP system, the patent system in Venice and then the first corporate statutes may have been birthed during the Renaissance and Age of Enlightenment but came into maturity during the Industrial Age, the 1880s. It therefore reflects the economic architecture of that period. Then came computers and the digital revolution about 100 years later. Software became critical. Algorithms became enormously valuable.
Data became an essential economic resource. The Internet transformed reproduction and distribution. The IP system adapted. Here at WIPO, for example, the WIPO Internet Treaties of the 1990s which will celebrate the 30th anniversary in a few weeks’ time were a very important and rapid response to those digital transformations. Much of this adaptation has involved adding layers on to an existing architecture whose basic categories were developed from earlier industrial economy without having to rethink the architecture.
AI is forcing us to turn our attention to the underlying architecture and to ask ourselves fundamental questions about its continued relevance. Who is an inventor when AI makes a material contribution to an invention? Who is the author when human creativity and machine generation become increasingly intertwined? On what basis under what conditions should copyright protected material be used for AI training? What are the remuneration and compensation models?
How can we say we respect copyright and yet pay nothing for it? How should we think about software algorithms and data as sources of economic value? We are now confronting something even more fundamental. What are the attributes of human identity itself? Our voices, our images, our likenesses, our biometric characteristics, even our thoughts.
AI can replicate these in ways that earlier generations could barely have imagined. When technology is sufficiently advanced it is indistinguishable from magic. Yet the legal protections surrounding them remain fragmented across IP, privacy, personality rights, unfair competition and other bodies of law. Indeed, this afternoon the forum asked directly whether the IP system has a role in protecting not only what humans make but what makes us human. I don’t pretend that any of these questions has an easy answer.
We are not here just to tackle easy questions. Second, how should the IP system itself change? Even if we conclude that the basic architecture of IP remains sound, there is another challenge. The system of IP registration and protection which we must remember is a starting point for IP commercialization has to operate at the speed of the innovators and creators and the economies and societies that it serves. Much of today’s IP regime and infrastructure was built around industrial innovation cycles measured in the lifespan of years.
Digital innovation cycles operates much faster and AI will accelerate these cycles even further. Imagine an entrepreneur building a company whose AI enabled technology fundamentally changes several times during the period in which an IP right is being examined. Imagine IP offices confronted with vastly increased volumes of AI assisted applications or expanding bodies on machine generated prior art. Imagine creators trying to license millions of machine mediated users through transaction models designed for another era. The question is, therefore, not only whether we are able to protect what is valuable in the age of AI but also whether the machinery of IP protection is fast enough, accessible enough and adaptable enough for the AI enabled innovators and creators it now has to serve.
If we do not get this right, we will find ourselves in a situation where innovators and creators will find that the IP system simply does not serve them anymore. They will not file and then some of them have told me their IP strategy will increasingly be speed to market. So we need to have a frank conversation about what new processes, timelines and procedures need to be put in place for the IP system to remain relevant in a world where innovation and business cycles move not just in years but increasingly in months and weeks. Third, how do we make the economics work? Perhaps this is the most practical question of all.
AI depends on enormous quantities of knowledge, culture, information and data. That value has been created by human beings and creators rightly want recognition and sustainable livelihoods. At the same time, innovators and AI companies need the ability to develop and train powerful models. Researchers need room to experiment. Businesses need predictable and workable rules.
Consumers want access to better and more affordable products and services. Society needs both continued human creativity and continued technological innovation. These interests will sometimes conflict as they have in the past few years. But we should resist reducing this debate into a simple contest between creators and technology or between those who want protection and those who want access. IP has spent centuries dealing with precisely this part of problems, how to create incentives while enabling ideas to circulate, how to protect the current generation of creators while enabling the future generation of creators to emerge.
So the question cannot simply be who has the legal power to say no. We must also ask how can we create workable ways for people to say yes. That means exploring new licensing practices, new remuneration mechanisms, better metadata and rights information, technical solutions for attribution and provenance and new business relationships between creators, rights holders and AI developers. That is one reason why WIPO created the AI infrastructure interchange in March this year, providing a neutral space where creators, rights holders, technology developers and technical experts can work on practical questions including metadata, water marking, identifiers and rights management infrastructure. Because law alone will not solve every problem.
Sometimes technology should be part of the solution to challenges created by technology. Sometimes a solution will not only be found in new laws and regulations but also in new market practices, new licensing models and new technical standards. This brings me to why we are here today, this morning. These questions cannot be addressed only by governments. The complexity and breadth of the topic means that creators, innovators, professionals, regulators, academia and civil society need to come together.
Because AI will not just change countries within national boundaries but the whole of humanity, this is work that needs to involve all 194 Member States. That is the purpose of this forum, to create a place where Member States and stakeholders can meet in a neutral, professional and inclusive platform to understand what is changing across the whole spectrum of innovative and creative experiences beyond any single IP right, exchange experiences and approaches and identify where future work may be needed. I hope we will disagree over these next two days. In fact, I would worry if we did not. I also hope that we can begin identifying where there is convergence.
Perhaps in a day and age where machines are becoming more like humans and humans are becoming more like machines, there should be principles on which we can agree even before we agree on every single rule, that human creativity should continue to matter, that human inventors and innovators should continue to be rewarded, that knowledge should continue to circulate, that creators and innovators should be able to participate fairly in the economic value they generate, that new technology should expand human possibility rather than diminish human agency and that countries should retain room to respond to their own circumstances while avoiding unnecessary fragmentation of a global ecosystem for supporting innovation and creativity. All of these may sound like modest points of agreement, but in a fragmented world, they may become a very important place to start. 500 years ago, societies began constructing institutions that connected human ingenuity to economic value on a systematic scale. Those institutions helped support extraordinary ways of innovation and creativity.
We are now approaching another critical juncture in human history, another once in 500 years moment. AI is beginning to change how ideas are created, how discoveries are made, how culture is produced and perhaps eventually how we understand invention, innovation and creativity. We should not fear that change, but neither should we simply surrender to it. Our responsibility is to shape it proactively. That requires something much more difficult than defending the past or predicting the future.
It requires us to decide what we want the future to be. It will require national experimentation and international cooperation. It requires us to be bold enough to ask whether the institutions built for an earlier age are ready for the one now arriving and to build a new one with today’s human innovator and creator, the modern narratives of the ancient human instinct of innovation and creativity with the human creator and innovator remaining at our center. This is the work I hope we can all begin together. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Director General, Excellencies, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen.

session_title: Chair Remarks
speaker: H.E. Mr. Kairat Torebayev
affiliation: Permanent Representative of the Republic of Kazakhstan to the World Trade Organization and international economic organizations, Kazakhstan
text:
I would like to add my welcome to this International Global Forum on Intellectual Property and Artificial Intelligence. Over these two days we will consider how the IP systems can continue to support innovation, creativity and public interest as AI transforms our societies. It is an honor to chair these proceedings. Before we proceed and dive in to the discussions, I have to make a slight adjustment to our program. Due to the unforeseen last minute changes in timing, I will postpone the prerecorded messages from ministers and other officials and in my housekeeping remarks until after the first key presentation.
Perhaps that is a fitting way to begin the Forum on Artificial Intelligence by reminding ourselves how quickly things can change. One of the key questions we have to all face is how to prepare ourselves for the future that is arriving faster than we anticipated. One answer, of course, is to remain flexible and another is better understand what lies ahead. And that is precisely what the first presentation will help us to do. It is my pleasure to welcome Mr. Ren Ito, cofounder and chairman of Sakana AI to share his perspective on what lies ahead.
Mr. Ito, the floor is yours. Thank you so much for the very kind introduction and it is a great honor to be here.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: Mr. Hesham Azmi
text:

Ladies and gentlemen, Excellencies, Ministers and His Excellency, Director General of the World Intellectual Property Organization and dear colleagues, I would like to begin by expressing my sincere thanks and appreciation to the World Intellectual Property Organization, WIPO, for organizing this important dialogue and making the decisions and recommendations from this event. I had long expected to be with you in Geneva today, but I had the opportunity to meet with you today and that was not possible. Given that we are the International Organization of Intellectual Property, on the subject of the Geneva Conference, I would like to encourage you to get involved in the Asia-Pacific Summit of the IAEA on November 10th, 2018, in partnership with the Egyptian Department of Intellectual Property with the Egyptian website, ITL, and in participation with the Egyptian Intellectual Property Organization for the 16th and 18th November, which is being organized by WIPO under the Egyptian Intellectual
Property Bureau. It will take place from the sixth conference and it is being held by Mr. Daren Tang, the International Organization of International Protocols. This conference is an important opportunity to strengthen the regional and international dialogue on the issues that have been raised regarding the challenges that are being raised, which are the challenges that are being raised by the International International Programme and by the International Programme and the International Programme. As follows, the conference on the evening of November 19th, 9 he is the official Daren Tang, the Director General of the International Organization. This conference represents an important opportunity to strengthen the international dialogue regarding the evolving challenges facing copyright in the age of artificial intelligence and digital transformation.
Ladies and gentlemen, a transformation that is reshaping the ways we produce knowledge, develop innovations, create works and distribute them. While this transformation offers exceptional opportunity, it also raises complex questions regarding the protection of Intellectual Property rights and the use of protected works in training artificial intelligence systems and the attribution of AI generated outputs to their creators and determining their ownership. The challenge we face today is not a choice between protecting Intellectual Property and advancing artificial intelligence. It is about establishing a balanced framework, one that allows both to thrive and in this way we must ensure that technological progress respects legitimate rights and provides appropriate incentives for human creativity and innovation while encouraging responsible access to knowledge and technology. For Egypt, these issues are closely linked.
They are part of our national development priorities. The National Intellectual Property Strategy launched by Egypt in September 2022 along with the establishment of the Egyptian Intellectual Property Authority has laid the foundation for developing a more integrated and modern system and effective one. We are working within this framework. We are working to strengthen institutional governance and update the legislative framework and to increase the contribution of Intellectual Property to economic growth. We are also focusing on developing the creative industries.
We recognize that artificial intelligence calls for a reevaluation of some assumptions that underpin the existing Intellectual Property frameworks. Now, this issue should be based on evidence and thorough consultation and on a clear understanding of the interests of creators and researchers as well as innovators and technology developers. In fact, it should involve society as a whole. At the international level, we all agree that no single country can face these challenges alone. Therefore, we attach great importance to WIPO’s role in facilitating dialogue and the exchange of national expertise and identifying the areas where international cooperation can yield practical results.
It is equally important that developing countries have a significant voice in shaping emerging trends. These transformations should not lead to a widening of the technological gap and the existing economic disparities. Rather, we must ensure that artificial intelligence enables countries to develop their innovative capabilities and strengthen their creative industries. And to realize greater economic and social value from Intellectual Property assets, ladies and gentlemen, let me take this opportunity to express my gratitude for the trust placed in me by selecting me to chair the leadership dialogue for information technology for the next two years, 2027 and 2028. I view this not only as a personal honor but also as a reflection of Egypt’s commitment to making an active contribution in the international dialogue on the future of Intellectual Property as I look forward to working with my colleagues from all over the world to foster a constructive exchange of ideas regarding the challenges and opportunities presented by artificial intelligence and to help build bridges of understanding between different perspectives and national priorities.
Egypt reaffirms its constant readiness to work with WIPO and Member States to ensure that Intellectual Property remains the driving force for human creativity. Dear colleagues and friends, thank you for the opportunity to be with you today virtually and to share Estonia’s message.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: H.E. Ms. Liisa-Ly Pakosta
text:
And thank you WIPO to bring us all together to discuss this very urgent and important topic, AI and Intellectual Property. We share responsibility to solve the things in advance ongoingly and not to do it as only aftermath. We all agree we are already living at AI era and this means that solving problems, creating things, images, texts, whatever, looks like differently today than it was yesterday. Intellectual Property must be an integral part of AI conversations. It must be in the middle of it and I would like to underline ahead of it.
Because people must remain in the center. It is the human mind, the human creator who must get the profit from the project he or she is managing. It means that we have to debate about authorship and inventorship in the way that there is a clear line in between the instrument and the human mind behind it. And this means clearly that the creator’s rights are in fair balance between protection and access to knowledge. In Estonia we have AI at schools.
It means that teachers and pupils together with academia test the use and creation with AI tools while they are studying. They also create new ways of studying throughout the AI era and possibilities. But this is also a very good learning tool. I very much believe that from very early age kids need education on their Intellectual Property, Intellectual Property in more general, but also AI and Intellectual Property. The third topic I would like to touch is the access to AI tools.
AI has already such an impact globally that we should consider it similarly to access to water. It means that especially small and medium size enterprises or creators on their own should need open source possibilities to create using the best that human kind has to offer with AI. Otherwise the existing digital divide will grow very vastly and this would be the result we would not be happy about. It means we have to avoid it definitely. And it is WIPO to offer here a global platform for discussions, global platform how to avoid digital divide, how to protect creators’ rights, but also how to innovate and support innovation in all these areas.
It means that everybody has to be included in to this dialogue. It means researchers and creators, politicians and entrepreneurs, but also young people. I mentioned kids, even the kids. Estonia is ready to share our experience and learn from others. Let’s build an Intellectual Property system that supports innovation, values, human creativity and ensures that benefits of AI are in our hands but the threats would be avoided.
I wish you open and forward looking and productive forum. Thank you so much.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: H.E. Ms. Mari-Leena Talvitie
text:
Dear participants, as minister responsible for copyright policy, I’m pleased to address this important global forum. We must ensure that copyright continues to support creativity and innovation in the age of AI. I warmly welcome this idea to bring experts and decision makers together. We need dialogue, shared understanding and international cooperation. One key area is infrastructure.
Finland has worked on that for many years with stakeholders, public authorities and international partners. Copyright infrastructure should be seen as a symbol and natural as a supermarket. No one questions that products on shelf have prices and descriptions. The same principle should apply to creative content. Clear and reliable information benefits everyone.
This helps creators and rightsholders manage their rights, license their works and receive payment for their efforts. It also supports innovation and legal access to content. Another important issue is the protection of identity. AI can imitate our voices, faces and other personal traits. Nonauthorized use homes and creators as well as politicians, public figures and ordinary citizens.
People must remain in control of how they likeness and identity are used. Clear rules and effective tools are needed. The digital transformation will continue for many years and no country can address these challenges alone. I hope WIPO will continue its strong coordinating role. I wish you productive discussions and every success for this forum.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: H.E. Mr. Kim Yong Sun
text:
I would like to congratulate WIPO on hosting the global forum on IP and AI and thank the Director General and the WIPO team for bringing everyone together to discuss an important issue of the AI era. Although I cannot join you in person, I’m pleased to have this opportunity to share Korea’s experience and policies on this topic. The first is improving IP administration and services through AI. Our ministry is moving towards AI based examination systems using specialized AI models developed in-house. We have already introduced AI into patent searches, trademark classification and design image searches to improve examination quality and we will continue to expand its use to other areas.
To make IP information more accessible to the public, we also plan to introduce an AI powered assistant that explains complex patent documents in plain language. The second is responding to the growing number of AI assisted IP applications. AI has significantly lowered the barriers to filing IP applications. In the first half of 2026, patent filings by individuals in Korea increased by 130% compared to last year. However, as filing becomes easier, we are also seeing a rise in low quality or fraudulent IP applications involving the misuse of AI referred to as IP slop.
To address this problem, our ministry has introduced an early screening system that detects such applications and sends out alerts. We also plan to review our fee system for individual applicants to discourage excessive filings resulting from low application costs. In addition, we will pursue legal and institutional reforms to address the misuse of AI during the application process such as the manipulation of experimental data. These measures will include invalidating patents and imposing financial penalties for such misconduct. And lastly, we are preparing our IP system for the future of AI.
Our ministry will look ahead to the changes AI will bring to the way we work, assess how it will affect our organizational structure and administrative operations and develop strategies accordingly. We also intend to establish the basic principles for AI in intellectual property for AI users and businesses in the IP field to promote responsible AI use and ensure that clear accountability remains with the people. We believe these efforts should go beyond individual countries and become a shared international initiative. Through close cooperation, IP offices can work together to harmonize their systems and develop new international norms in the age of AI. In this spirit, we would like to propose that WIPO take the lead in developing a set of common principles that all Member States can refer to when shaping their IP policies.
AI is bringing a wave of change we have never seen before. The direction we choose to take will determine whether this wave becomes a challenge or an opportunity. I hope starting with this forum, we will work together to find a way forward for IP in the age of AI and make meaningful progress. Thank you very much.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: H.E. Mr. Edwin Tong
text:
Director General Daren Tang, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, I’m sorry I can’t join you in person. Unfortunately, for all its advances, AI still cannot put me in two different places at the same time. Thankfully, technology allows me to deliver this prerecorded speech and I’m delighted to share some thoughts with you. First, I thank WIPO for convening this important inaugural global forum. AI is fundamentally transforming how we create and innovate, challenging our very basic assumptions underlying our IP systems.
I think we cannot nor should we stand in the way of progress. As policymakers, our task is to ensure that AI and IP reinforce rather than undermine each other so that innovation and human creativity can thrive together. I would like to suggest three areas where we can work together. First, sustaining human creativity alongside AI innovation. AI models learn from vast quantities of human created content, whilst increasingly generating content themselves.
How do we encourage AI innovation without weakening incentives for human creativity? Even before generative AI became mainstream, our copyright act in Singapore already permitted computational data analysis including AI training using lawfully accessed works subject to safeguards. Our approach is to regulate with a light touch, particularly when technology is evolving so rapidly. This we believe encourages innovation. We also believe in giving creators and innovators the space to experiment, develop new ideas and bring them to market without being constrained by overly prescriptive rules.
At the same time, they must have the confidence that their works are protected. That’s the environment we are seeking to provide in Singapore, one that encourages innovation underpinned by a strong, predictable IP framework. But getting this balance right is an ongoing process. That’s why we recently launched a public consultation on AI and IP. We are seeking views on strengthening our legal framework, including how copyright should apply to AI training and outputs, how best to recognize human creativity in AI assisted works and how our patent framework should respond to AI assisted inventions.
I believe these are challenges all of us face and also all of us can tackle them together. For example, we can explore practical approaches to licensing and rights management that facilitate lawful AI development, protect creators’ rights and value human creativity. Second, making different national approaches work together. Countries will understandably adopt different approaches, but fragmented rules could create legal uncertainty and opportunities for regulatory arbitrage. As a small, open economy, Singapore places particular importance on a predictable, interoperable international IP system.
We need not agree on everything, but we can find common ground and make our different approaches work better together. Singapore is keen to contribute our experience. Through WIPO, we can explore common principles, develop guidance on different national approaches and find practical solutions to cross-border challenges. Third, ensuring AI expands opportunities for everyone. AI could give individuals and small businesses capabilities once reserved for larger organizations.
Yet, concentrated control over data, computing power and IP could limit these opportunities. We must, therefore, guard against anticompetitive practices that exclude smaller players, whilst helping them acquire the knowledge and expertise to harness AI and manage their IP effectively. Singapore has long supported international capacity building in IP. This April, for example, we partnered WIPO to organize an executive program on emerging AI and IP challenges, bringing together professionals from nine countries. As Singapore assumes the ASEAN Chairmanship next year, we look forward to building on such initiatives to help more businesses and creators harness AI.
Our longstanding partnerships with WIPO and IP offices around the world reflect our belief that we achieve more by learning from one another and then combining our strengths. IP was designed to serve human ingenuity. We must ensure that it can continue to do so even in the age of AI. I thank all of you for the opportunity to speak, and I wish you fruitful discussions. I hope to join you in person at the next forum.
Thank you.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: Mr. Kasai Yasuyuki
text:
Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen, good morning. My name is Yasuyuki Kasai, Commissioner of the Japan Patent Office, JPO. First of all, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to Director General Tang and to all those concerned for providing us with a wonderful opportunity. Today, the world is at a major turning point driven by the rapid advancement of AI. In July of this year, the Government of Japan developed Japan’s growth strategy.
In addition to serving as Commissioner of the JPO, I was responsible for its development as a member of the Cabinet Secretariat. In the strategy, we have selected 17 strategic fields with a projected total scale of domestic, public and private investment expected to exceed 373 yen or approximately 2.33 US dollars cumulatively by fiscal year 2040. Within this framework, the AI transformation position adds an accelerator for growth. Accordingly, several core fields essential for this transformation including AI and semiconductors have been prioritized. By the end of the year, we will formulate the Japan’s growth strategy implementation plan which will include the details and amounts of domestic investment over the next five years leading up to around 2030.
While the Government of Japan positioned AI transformation as an accelerator of growth, the JPO is responding to the rapid development of AI by ensuring that our examination practice is future ready as well as reviewing our institutional frameworks. In Japan, patent applications for AI-related inventions stood at approximately 8,000 in 2019 but exceeded 20,000 in 2024. To address the rapid growth of these applications, the JPO launched the AI examination support team in 2021 to provide support for their examination. In addition, the JPO is promoting the use of AI and its operations and released the JPO AI vision this July. The AI vision advocates a human centric approach as one of its key concepts aiming for the responsible use of AI.
Through these ongoing efforts, the JPO has keenly reaffirmed the importance of a deep collaboration with stakeholders and taking into consideration trend in the foreign countries regarding AI. As AI rapidly advances, it is essential for Member States and stakeholders to come together and share diverse experience, insights and challenges in order to ensure that IP administrations and the IP system continue to support global innovation and creativity. This global platform truly responds to the demand of the times by providing a cross-cutting platform for the dialogue on IP and AI. I would like to pay my sincere respect to WIPO for organizing this forum. Unfortunately, I could not join you today.
Instead, Mr. Nunaka, Deputy Commissioner of the JPO is attending on our behalf. Through this forum and other endeavors, the JPO remains fully committed to contributing to the global discussions on AI and Intellectual Property. Thank you very much for your attention.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: H.E. Mr. Kamal Shehadi
text:
Director General Daren Tang, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen, it is an honor to join you at the first global forum on Intellectual Property and Artificial Intelligence. I’m sorry I cannot be with you in Geneva, but I’m glad to open this conversation with you from Beirut. I would like to thank WIPO and Director General Tang for creating this space. Artificial Intelligence is moving faster than most legal frameworks were built to handle. A forum that brings Member States and stakeholders together regularly and openly is exactly what this moment needs.
The questions before you are not small. They are the questions of the age. Who is the author of a work created with AI? Who is the discoverer of something an algorithm helped discover? What happens to the rights of creators whose work is used to train these systems?
Each answer will shape how people create, invest and share knowledge for decades to come. In Lebanon, we live and deal with these questions from a particular vantage point. We are a country with a long tradition of creativity, entrepreneurship and talent. Our engineers, designers, writers and founders work around the world. At the same time, we are building our own digital foundation and developing our approach to AI at home.
We know that Intellectual Property cannot be an afterthought. It is what lets a young innovator in Beirut, Tripoli or Saida believe that an idea can become a business and that the business can grow without the idea being taken from them. We also know that no country can answer these questions alone. Large economies and smaller ones, those that build AI and those that mostly use AI all have a stake in shaping the rules. Smaller countries need a voice in shaping those rules and not only the task of adhering to them.
This is why forums like this one matter. I would like to leave you with three hopes for the next two days. First, that we protect creators and innovators so that people keep being rewarded and incentivized to create original work. Second, that we keep the door open to progress so that AI can serve healthcare, education, public services and economic growth. Third, that we make sure every Member State, whatever its size or resources, takes part in this conversation on equal terms.
Lebanon is ready to listen, to learn and to contribute. We value our partnership with WIPO and we look forward to working with you.

session_title: Ministerial-level Remarks
speaker: H.E. Mr. Ziyambi Ziyambi
text:
I wish you a productive and inspiring forum. Thank you. Mr. Director General, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, ladies and gentlemen, at the outset I wish to extend my highest commendations to the World Intellectual Property Organization and to you, Mr. Director General, for your visionary leadership in convening this inaugural global forum on Intellectual Property and Artificial Intelligence. By transitioning from exploratory dialogues to this structured, inclusive and multilateral platform, WIPO has fostered a collaborative space where all nations actively participate in shaping the global governance of Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property. In doing so, this forum provides a vital opportunity to move beyond theory, allowing us to exchange concrete best practices, harmonize regulatory insights and collaborative architect a jurisprudence that is balanced, equitable globally and globally aligned.
Earlier this year, Zimbabwe proudly launched its national Artificial Intelligence strategy for 2026 to 2030. We do not view AI merely as a novel technology but as a catalyst for inclusive growth, enhanced public service delivery and economic diversification. While the state will fulfill its duty to provide robust regulatory direction and enabling legal environment, the true Vanguard of this revolution will be the unyielding creativity of our people, nurtured within our universities and propelled by our private sector. Zimbabwe’s vision is rooted in fostering local agency and authorship within this digital economy, a principle that serves as the bedrock of our national Artificial Intelligence strategy. This strategy does not merely seek to adopt technology.
It intentionally builds domestic capacity across critical pillars from sustainable digital infrastructure to targeted human capital development. Our young innovators are already translating this policy into practice, pioneering localized solutions to uniquely domestic challenges. A prime example is crop fix, an AI-enabled pest and disease diagnostic tool developed by a youth-led startup. To sustain this momentum, we are aggressively investing in human capital through our new software developer skills development hub and specialized trainings for agricultural extension offices. However, for this ecosystem to thrive, our legal frameworks must keep pace.
Our current copyright and patent laws were not designed for the complexities of the digital age, making IP reform our most immediate priority. Mr. DG, the primary legislation governing Intellectual Property rights for creators, performers and broadcasts organization in Zimbabwe is the copyright and neighboring rights act, chapter 26.05. The act defines an author strictly as an individual. Consequently, works generated entirely by AI face a legal vacuum. Therefore, the law must urgently clarify ownership rights and define the threshold of human input required for legal protection.
Furthermore, Mr. DG, AI training models rely on the consumption of vast datasets. Our regulatory framework remains silent on whether fair dealing exemptions cover commercial AI training. Our creators require absolute assurance of credit and compensation just as our developers need clear, predictable rules to innovate with confidence. Our legislation also defines an inventor as the natural person who devised the invention, leaving AI unrecognized. While global consensus largely favors human inventorship, the landscape remains fragmented.
We must determine how to assign ownership when researchers, AI developers and data owners all contribute to a single breakthrough. Additionally, the black box nature of AI complicates patent disclosure requirements and our laws must carefully delineate between an unpatentable algorithm and a patentable technical solution such as an AI system that improves crop yields or diagnosis of diseases. Crucially, Zimbabwe stresses the urgent need to protect traditional knowledge, cultural expressions and African data. AI systems consume vast datasets. We must, therefore, enforce mechanisms for consent, recognition and equitable benefit sharing, ensuring that local communities are never marginalized.
Mr. Director General, Zimbabwe does not face these questions in isolation. If nations fragment into divergent regulatory frameworks, cross-border innovation will stall under the weight of legal uncertainty. International cooperation has always been the cornerstone of IP consistency and the dawn of AI makes collaboration more critical than ever. Our collective mission is to architect an Intellectual Property system that is innovative yet balanced, technologically responsive yet profoundly human centric and protective of rights while supportive of public access. We must ensure that AI serves to bridge rather than widen the digital divide, empowering developing nations to create, evaluate and participate fully in the global knowledge economy.
Zimbabwe looks forward to collaborating closely with WIPO, fellow Member States and all global stakeholders to ensure our international Intellectual Property system remains resilient, equitable and fit for the edge of artificial intelligence. I thank you.

session_title: Tech Radar: Ready or Not - AI's Next Frontier
speaker: Mr. Ren Ito
affiliation: Co-founder and Chairman, Sakana AI, Japan
text:
Director General Tan, excellencies, colleagues, friends, good morning. Thank you once again for inviting me at this inaugural global Forum on IP and AI. When WIPO invited me to give this 10 minutes’ talk on the next frontier of AI, I did what you expect someone who runs an AI company would do. I asked my own AI a few ideas. Some had already occurred to me.
Others of ideas would never have crossed my mind. But within seconds I had almost enough material to cover both days of this Forum as you can imagine. So what exactly will be my job this morning? First, let me speak about how far has AI come so far. Take the overall performance of foundational models across a range of standard mass, coding, reasoning and those benchmarks to give you a rough sense of the scale.
If we take the 2019 level as 1, the figure is rising to about 50 in 2023 and about 1,000 in 2026. That’s the numerical reality. But what those numbers mean actually in practice? In my company we are building a system called AI scientist. Give it a research topic and it designs and runs experiments.
Interpret the results and writes a paper. As an experiment, we submitted three of its papers to a workshop at ICLR, an international AI research conference. And boom, one of the three papers passed a peer review by the human researchers. So this is a good example to understand and discuss what would we actually like to hand over to AI. You know, what is the kind of the work we are happy to give up and give it to the AI?
Two kinds of the work can easily come up in my mind. The first one is there is work I can do myself but will happily hand over. Take my expense report after a trip like this one. I got an electronic hotel invoice in my inbox, a hand written taxi receipt almost unreadable in my pocket and a credit card statement in hundreds of different currencies. I can match it up manually but I will be delighted if AI can do that for me.
Easy. Then there is another kind of work I could never do on my own. Imagine a pharmaceutical company looking for a better way to deliver a drug. This is a true story. By searching patents across industries, AI might stop a small materials company whose technology could help and now there is an acquisition idea worth exploring.
I could spend my whole career reading all those patent documents and never make that connection between the pharmaceutical company who might want to acquire that material company. That’s the power of AI going beyond the current human capacity. I love AI to help me spot an acquisition opportunity like that but would I let AI decide whether to buy that company? What is the threshold? Pope, Leo XIX makes a point about responsibility.
AI can imitate empathy but it has no conscience of its own. Suppose I take the AI’s advice like that and buy this company. If the deal goes badly and the people lose their jobs, I cannot stand in front of those employees and say, you know what, the AI thought it was a good idea. This is why I made a decision. No. I have to answer for it.
Another example, it is not a pope but Henry Kissinger. He raised a question in his 2018 essay titled how the enlightenment ends. Suppose AI gives us an answer that works and we use it even though we do not understand how it got there. We solved the problem but how much have we actually learned? Of course, let me give you one example.
Of course, I’m happy to get on a plane even though I cannot fully explain everything that keeps in the air. But part of the reason I trust the aviation is that if something goes wrong, there are people who can work out what happened and decide what needs to change. It is not a complete black box. When we rely on AI, what we need are the people who can do that, too. The question pope was asking is about who takes the responsibility for decision.
Kissinger is asking how well we understand the answers AI is giving us. Let’s go back to my lab example. How would those two questions look like in the lab setting? Imagine this AI system which is suggesting 100 different experiments. One looks especially promising, but a human researcher remembers that trying something similar like that 10 years ago and she knows why it failed.
Even if it was seemingly optimistic from her experience 10 years ago, she knows that that failed. So she takes another idea on the list, changes one condition or two and runs the experiment and boom, this time it works. The AI is suggesting these experiments and she is figuring out what had to change to make it work. If all we record is her final sign-off only, if we are shrinking the scope of our conversation and only looking at her final sign-off, that insight disappears from the story. So here is my question to you.
Could we think about those AI, the IP system as a way to record human judgment throughout the creative process? When people invent with AI, how can the IP system capture the judgments they make along the way so we can see what each person actually contributed? We have been talking now about what people contribute when they work with AI. But let me finish with a much simpler question and much harder question. Is there anything which only a human being can do?
The last time I met Darren, he told me about the piece of music he heard. He liked it. Then partway through, something felt a little off. Darren looked it up and discovered it had been made with AI. Good instinct as a musician.
Talented DG with a musical background. But that conversation led me to tell him about Nina Simone, an American jazz singer and pianist who was a star in the 1960s. There is a film before sunset. At the end of the film before sunset, Celine, played by Julie Delpy, puts on Nina Simone’s recording of Just in Time. She sways to the music and does a little impression of Simone.
I loved that scene so much that I was looking for Simone’s live recordings on YouTube, 100 and 200 of the different live recordings. And I found myself listening for the way she makes you wait just a little longer for the next row. Hundreds of different live performances are all different. AI itself can put chords together, make harmonious or cacophonious, whatever chords. It can play a little behind the beat.
But what moves me is the way Celine borrows the gestures and the voice of a singer she loves. Of all the ways she could express herself in that moment, that’s the one she chooses. And in that choice, you see something of who she is. Let me come back to where I started. What was my job this morning?
AI gave me tons of ideas to cover for both days of this forum. My part was to choose which of them to talk about and in what order. And it was up to me to explain why those choices matter to me and why I saw they might matter to you. I chose to leave you with Nina Simone and that was my job this morning. And Darren, I did have one other reason.
I wanted to see if you remembered our conversation. So thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Ito, for that fascinating glimpse into the next frontier of artificial intelligence and for helping us better understand what might lie ahead and so we can choose better.

session_title: Showcase 1: AI in Action - From Ideas to Real-World Impact
speaker: Chair
text:
We have just heard interventions and we also had a keynote from Mr. Ito which gave us a fascinating glimpse into what artificial intelligence may be capable of tomorrow but what can it already make possible today. That is what our AI in action showcase are all about. Over these two days we will see how AI is helping us tackle some of humanity’s biggest challenges. Problems that have remained beyond our reach despite decades of scientific progress. But we will also discover how innovators around the world are using AI to solve problems all around the world, turning local issues into real world solutions.
How AI is opening up entirely new possibilities for human creativity and expression. And we begin with one of the greatest challenges of all, human health. Imagine if a medical image could reveal clues invisible to even the most experienced specialists, clues that could help us understand understand cancer better, predict how a patient might respond to treatment and ultimately save lives. Our next guest is helping make that possible. Please welcome Professor Anand Madhava Hoshi, Executive Director of the Emory empathetic AI for Health Institute.
Professor, the floor is yours.

session_title: Showcase 1: AI in Action - From Ideas to Real-World Impact
speaker: Mr. Anant Madabhushi
affiliation: Executive Director of the Emory Empathetic AI for Health Institute and Robert W. Woodruff Professor of Biomedical Engineering, Emory University, United States of America
text:
Assistant Director General of WIPO, ministers, excellencies and dear colleagues, it is a pleasure to be here in Geneva this morning and a real pleasure to be giving this talk on artificial intelligence and health. And I very intentionally framed my presentation from pixels to patents to patients, translating interpretable AI for precision medicine. As you heard from the Assistant Director General, there is a huge opportunity to use the power of AI to clean patterns and features from routine medical images. Not just because these medical images can allow us to detect and diagnose diseases earlier, to really help radiologists identify early cues around cancer, but critically, there is a huge opportunity to use these images to find patterns, to find features that can help prognosticate outcomes and disease trajectories for patients with cancer. But perhaps even more critically, there is a huge opportunity to identify the ability to predict treatment response to specific drugs for patients with cancer because one of the big challenges that we have today is that all the drugs that are provided to cancer patients do not have 100% efficacy.
In fact, the majority of these drugs only work in 20 to 25% of cancer patients. And the ability of artificial intelligence coupled with routinely acquired data allows the opportunity to realize the promise of precision medicine, which is bearing the right treatment with the right patient to achieve the best possible outcome. You heard this morning that one of the big challenges with artificial intelligence is that it tends to be fairly black boxed. In other words, we don’t always understand what the features are, how the AI is coming up with its representations, with its predictions. Now, that might be okay when for many, many different applications you heard from our keynote speaker this morning for looking at your tables or your travel adjustments, it might be okay.
But when it comes to health, interpretability becomes really critical to drive trust both from a physician and a patient perspective. The other issue with the black box nature of a lot of AI is this issue of lack of reproducibility of the AI. We saw this during the pandemic when a number of AI algorithms to identify COVID were released. Unfortunately, none of them turned out to be generalizable resulting in this issue of AI slop, the lack of reproducibility around AI. And that is a big challenge and directly connected to the fact that the AI algorithms don’t really we don’t really understand the source of the features or the patterns with respect to how the AI is making its predictions.
One of the other challenges also with the AI is that while the argument is made that more data can help the AI algorithms, the irony is that the more data that’s fed to these algorithms, the higher the likelihood that they can hallucinate. And this is a term I think a lot of us have become very familiar with where AI can give very, very compelling responses to questions that are completely erroneous. My wife who works in the financial space and doesn’t really work in the AI, I was trying a few months ago to explain to her this concept of AI hallucination. We were sitting in bed and she was reading something and sort of indulging me, not really engaged in my conversation around AI hallucinations. At which point I pulled out my laptop.
I dropped in a picture of myself. And to my great surprise, chat GPT told me here that this photo is a picture of Dr. Anant Marabushi. And as you can see, those highlights are obviously my own. His work is highly recognized in the field of artificial intelligence and medical imaging. Very excitedly I looked at my wife and said, look, dear, chat GPT knows who I am.
At which point my wife’s smile looked at me and said, oh, dear, now I understand what you mean by AI hallucinating. But is there another way? And so in our group, we focused on the use of artificial intelligence not to make direct predictions but instead to focus on extracting patterns, to extract features from routine data, radiographic images like CT or MRI scans, biopsy images that can now be digitized. And now trying to associate these patterns that we’re capturing from routine data to questions around disease trajectories, patient outcomes and more critically predicting treatment response and treatment benefit. So what does this look like?
Here’s an example of a CT scan for a lung cancer patient. You can see a large adenocarcinoma or large lung mass in the bottom right lung. Now, this is on a CT scan, but with the power of AI, we can extract out this nodule. We can look at patterns inside the tumor, outside the tumor, but critically we can look at features associated with the vessels of the tumor. We can look at the twistedness and the tortuosity of the vessels associated with the tumor.
Now, assuming this individual gets a resection of the lung nodule, we actually saw an example of this with the pope who was diagnosed with early stage lung cancer recently and underwent resection. So that piece of tissue can now be digitized and with the power of AI, we can now start to analyze the patterns of cells on the biopsy image that is used for diagnosis. AI can identify the tissue areas. AI can identify exactly where the cancer is. AI can identify the individual cancer cells and allow us to transform this pathology image into a series of quantitative representations that capture the different patterns of cell abundance and cellular diversity.
And these patterns from the pathology images and the radiology images now allow us to start to connect treatment response and specific drug efficacy with cancer patients across a whole host of different cancers. And you can see multiple different cancer types over on your left, individual treatment categories like chemotherapy, immunotherapy in the middle and specific treatment combinations over on your right. And our group, a number of other groups are looking at the use of these algorithms to be able to associate for different cancer patients the right treatment that has the highest likelihood of treatment benefit. Now, why does this matter? Let’s take an example of hormonal receptor positive breast cancer, one of the most common breast cancers out there.
The challenge is that the vast majority of women with early stage breast cancer will actually do well without chemotherapy. But the question of which women will or should get chemotherapy versus those women that can avoid chemotherapy is still an open one. We have tests that can look at the tissue, but they destroy the tissue. They look at the gene expression and these can cost thousands of dollars. But what about a country like India where the cost of chemotherapy is about $1,900?
How do you afford a $4,000 test to tell you whether you need chemotherapy or not? So the opportunity is that if we can look at a digital image of a biopsy and find patterns of individual cells, we now have the opportunity to figure out exactly which women with breast cancer are going to benefit from chemotherapy and which women can safely avoid it. So essentially you now have a $5 test to be able to predict benefit of chemotherapy as compared to a $4,000 genomic test. But it’s not just hormonal receptor positive breast cancer. We can look at other types of breast cancers as well, HER2 positive breast cancers where you have so-called targeted therapies specifically directed to that particular breast cancer.
Our group has shown recently that we can now identify which women with HER2 positive breast cancer are going to benefit from Tristuzumab, which is a targeted therapy, finding patterns of immune cells on these biopsy images. The AI is able to identify a subset of patients that are truly going to benefit versus those women who are not going to benefit. Prostate cancer. President Joe Biden last year was diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer. One of the questions is which men with advanced prostate cancer will benefit from chemotherapy.
We addressed this question in a study that we published earlier this year. We are looking at just routine biopsy images. We were able to train an AI algorithm that looked at arrangement of immune cells and identified that there were specific subsets of patients with advanced prostate cancer who were going to benefit from the chemotherapy versus patients who were not going to benefit. Specifically, we found that when the AI was positive or the AI was over representing features of the immune cells, those patients would truly get benefit from chemotherapy. On the other hand, where the AI was not positive, those patients would not receive benefit.
If you look at that little table at the bottom there, you can see that when the AI was positive, patients who received chemotherapy had a 1.2 year survival benefit over patients who did not. So you can see the huge opportunity being able to identify the right treatment and avoiding chemotherapy for a lot of cancer patients. Now, I turned 50 earlier this year. And I suspect like a lot of you, your vision starts to go. So you have to go see your ophthalmologist on an annual exam and you get a fundus image.
Now, that fundus image is used to tell you whether your eye health is deteriorating. But the opportunity is much more. We’re able to look at these routine fundus images to ask questions not just about your eye health but potentially whether you have Alzheimer’s. What is your cardiovascular risk? What is your kidney disease risk?
In our group, we have been training AI algorithms that now are able to predict based of arrangement of blood vessels, 10 years out, your likelihood of developing hematologic malignancies, cancers like multiple myeloma, lymphoma, leukemia. There’s a study that we published last year where simply looking at vessel patterns in routine fundus images, 10 years before the actual diagnosis, the AI was able to predict the onset of these different cancers. And in fact, we have now extended this to looking at multiple different breast and female reproductive cancers. The AI is able to look at these images and predict 12 years out as to which women will go on to develop these different kinds of breast and reproductive cancers. So in these last few minutes, I wanted to come back to the issue of IP.
Over the last two decades, my group has very intentionally focused on developing an IP portfolio, not simply because it helps with the CV but really because of the focus on translation. And over the years, we have really worked to help build companies, to license technologies and try to sort of get these technologies to patients. But the question is what does one patent? And as you saw in my talk today, I have really focused on patenting not the algorithm but patenting the pattern instead. Vessels, twistedness, arrangement of individual cells, patterns that can then be linked to important treatment outcomes and patient trajectories.
So I’ll give you one specific example here in the last couple of minutes. QVT or quantitative vessel tortuosity was a pattern or a biomarker that we discovered in our group nearly nine years ago. The technology was identified in the lab to be shown to be strongly associated with outcome in cancer patients. We filed for IP. We wrote some of the seminal papers.
We then licensed the technology to a company, started a prospective trial with the technology, built the patent family around this new pattern and more recently got device breakthrough device designation from the FDA. A nine-year journey with the specific pattern that we identified but it’s taken nine years now to actually get it to patients and start ongoing clinical trials. But this came from the lab. This came based on observations, conversations with our clinicians, with our radiology colleagues to start the discovery that with the AI we were able to find features, patterns related to the blood vessels that could look at breast cancer patients and based of the twistedness of the blood vessels we could predict which breast cancer patients were going to benefit from chemotherapy. We found that the smoother the vessels, the more likely they would respond favorably to chemotherapy, the more twisted they were, the less likely they were to respond.
We have now shown this also in the context of lung cancer patients, specifically which patients will benefit from immunotherapy versus chemotherapy and similar to the work in breast cancer, we have shown that the more twisted the blood vessels, the more likely these patients are to not benefit from immunotherapy. The smoother they are, the more likely they are to benefit from immunotherapy. But it’s not just the retrospective validation. It’s really critical with these technologies to bring it to patients through the use of prospective clinical trials and that’s exactly what we are doing with this ongoing clinical trial where the QVT technology is now being prospectively validated in lung cancer patients. We don’t know the outcome of the trial yet, but when the trial reads out, we will be able to associate the QVT biomarker with patient survival, with patient trajectories.
But this is the kind of prospective validation that’s really critical to take the technology from conception, patent, to ultimately translation to patients. So with that, I would like to just end with some takeaways. One, hopefully I have conveyed that AI on routine images can transform precision medicine. Secondly, when we talk about IP, let’s focus on patenting the pattern, not necessarily the algorithm. IP is the bridge from paper to patient, but only if it generalizes and that’s where the validation is so absolutely critical.
And finally, we have to build democratization into the IP strategy so that these licensing models can be kept low cost and accessible, particularly in low and middle income countries. Thank you very much. And I just wanted to do a quick shout out to the amazing students and faculty and postdocs that I have the pleasure and honor of working with. Thank you very much.

session_title: Super Session: Back to First Principles - Is the IP System Fit for the Age of AI?
speaker: Mr. Stanley Lai
affiliation: Head of the IP Practice, Allen & Gledhill LLP, Singapore
text:
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Good morning, everyone. It is a pleasure to see all of you here. As I recall what the Director General was saying this morning about this being the 30th anniversary of the Internet Treaties 1996, it actually was a celebratory reminder to me that that’s as long as I have been practicing Intellectual Property law and it shows. As the head of the IP practice in one of Singapore’s largest firms, it is my pleasure today to actually appear before all of you and I’m very pleased to be able to introduce a very esteemed panel of speakers.
Before that, let me just say a few words in terms of the introduction to this session. The IP system has traditionally rested on a number of key principles, including the encouragement of innovation and also the protection of an individual’s natural rights over his or her creations. The proliferation of artificial intelligence and the peculiarities has prompted us in recent years to confront some of these principles and explore the extent to which they remain relevant today. So I propose to divide the time that we have with this panel into two segments. First of all, I will invite each speaker whom I’m about to introduce imminently to share their respective positions on the topic.
Then after that, I will ask the speakers to engage in a structured exchange to tease out some of the perspectives and tensions where our ideas and principles collide and in some way it sets the stage for the rest of this conference where we try to find the answers to that. Now, actually, there are seven speakers, excluding myself. We have actually Mr. Anthony Taubman who is the Director of IP at WTO and he actually is joining us online. Tony, I hope you can hear us. I certainly can’t see you, but I hope you can see us and you will be able to answer the questions.
Secondly, I’m also pleased to introduce at the far end of this panel Mr. Cedric Manara, who is the Director and Head of Copyright at Google. Two spaces down, ladies and gentlemen, we didn’t actually take any particular order, but two spaces down from Cedric’s right would be Mirtha Rivas, who is the General Counsel of Nestle. Next to her on her left, and I know this is starting to get confusing, but please get used to it, Professor Gatan, who is an Associate Professor of Science, Technology and Innovation Policy at the Swiss Federal Technology Institute of La Salle. And to Mirtha’s right is Professor Chijoke Okori, who is an Associate Professor of Law at the University of Pretoria. Her expertise lies in IP, AI data science and African development, and that’s the key.
We need to get the perspective of the global south on this as well. So let’s make a start. Anthony, can you hear me? I’m not sure whether he can. Yes, indeed, Stanley. Very good to see you.
Yes. I’m just going to ask you to kick us off because I think the theme we want to talk about is IPs of philosophical foundations and whether the international architecture as we know it and as you have worked on it for many, many years, that’s how I have known you, can absorb AI and IPs’ justifications draw on Locke’s labor, Hegel’s personality and also Bentham’s utility. Those of us who know this will know this. The Greeks distinguish poesis or the making from mimesis which is the imitation. AI is arguably the most powerful mimetic engine ever built.
