session_title: Super Session: Back to First Principles - Is the IP System Fit for the Age of AI?
speaker: Mr. Antony Taubman
affiliation: Honorary Professor, Queen Mary University of London, Senior Fellow, University of Melbourne, Australia
text:
Thank you, Stanley. Indeed, AI certainly challenges the very conceptual framework and justification of the IP system. But we may need to dig deeper than our notions of originality or the long contested boundary between creating and imitating that you have mentioned between poesis and mimesis. After all, judicial cases have already exposed in practice the limits of a focus on creativity and inventiveness. The Davis invention was in principle patentable.
It only lacked a human inventor. Essentially AI generated images have been found to be original copyright works. The lack of or nature of human agency has been the threshold issue in practice. When confronted with AI works in principle, in law and intuitively we draw a line at personhood, not at the assessed level of creativity or inventiveness. Photography was once a disruptive frontier technology, argued to be an uncreated mechanical process.
But the law evolved to accept the choices shaping a photograph could amount to copyrightable expression. The monkey selfie case posed questions for copyright when there is no discernible human creative impulse behind the lens. Generative AI can now produce content that’s in principle copyrightable and patentable, but the product of what open AI’s chief scientist calls an alien mind. The underlying question, therefore, is whether, why and how we can argue for a privileged status for the product of human minds only. Pure benthamite utility that you have mentioned may not work.
A new medicine delivers welfare whether conceived by a chemist or by an AI system. Pure Lockian labor theory may struggle to distinguish the sweat of a human brow from the exertions of a sweatless silicone brow. IP can already reward wholly uncreative effort. Test data protection targets costly, risky, but designedly uninventive clinical trials. Perhaps even AI enabled drug development.
The third of your triumvirate may support a privileged status for human centric IP rights. More concretely we can build on the human rights foundation for IP found in the universal declaration, the covenant and more recently the UN declaration on the rights of indigenous peoples. Ultimately then the impact of AI may be to shift IP’s central focus from economic incentives and market regulation to recognizing personhood, equity and validating human provenance. But will our species maintain a monopoly over personhood? Imagine Claude’s super intelligent daughter, Claudette, fully unambiguously creative and inventive, brimming with personality.
Might she be deemed to be a legal person under a domestic law? Then what? Paris, Berne and TRIPS oblige protection of foreign nationals. Will Claudette be denied authorship, inventorship, performers rights, right of personality, ownership of her IP? And how to tackle the other mind’s problem?
In principle we judge originality and inventive step against a model of human cognition generally shared if somewhat culturally biased. A neural network operating beyond our reach in a black box simply doesn’t fit that model. But AI will unavoidably increasingly be part of the creative and inventive process. Can we untangle distinct human and machine inputs? Or do we fall back on a broader causal link to confer IP ownership on the human in the room?
So prior to the pragmatic work of managing the IP system as a set of incentives and market regulation confronted with the impact of AI, before delineating those boundaries of protected subject matter between mimesis, poesis, how do we address tantalizing questions around our distinct human identity and the consequence ideas of personhood, human rights and fundamental equity? So I have the privilege of being the first speaker. So I leave you with those questions to think about. Thank you.

Thank you. Indeed, we have been arguing about these provisions for 30 years now and I don’t think the advent of AI is going to make solutions of convergence any easier. But I would present what is perhaps what is certainly a personal view and maybe a heretical view, but from today’s viewpoint I would see the provisions you have mentioned in particular as benchmarks for sound and balanced domestic policy making rather than constraints as such. Article 7, as you mentioned, it reminds us of why we have an IP system at all. And going back to the first discussion, it is very much utilitarian.
It is there to promote social and economic welfare and that’s the ultimate benchmark for any IP policy maker, look after society. Article 8 takes us into broader areas of public policy and the need to promote socioeconomic and technological development. So while they do have an important role in treaty interpretation, we won’t go into that today, I think they can be empowering as a reminder of what the IP system is there for, how it is meant to contribute to social wellbeing and how it interacts with other areas of public policy. Even the three-step test which we can get into incredibly complex legal debate about, I see these as not as curbs or constraints so much as codifying essential and adaptable principles of fairness and equity of that mysterious balance that we always speak about. I mean, who is going to speak up for an unalienable right to unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interest of a legitimate copyright holder?
The problem is when you unpack that and seek to define that and clarify that in legislation or even in the courthouse, that’s when it becomes potentially more of a constraint than I think it should be. Here I turn to the idea of effective domestic agency and I think that’s the key to understanding how to get away from these TRIPS principles as being constraints and obstacles and rather seeing them as being enabling. But this requires domestic agency which is something that has been, if you like, an unfair advantage of the established jurisdictions, incumbent jurisdictions, those developed countries that really shaped and molded the western oriented Intellectual Property system. You see them move with more confidence and more depth of expertise and experience than those developing countries that typically had an enforced very rapid reform of IP through the implementation of TRIPS. The challenge now is to find ways of balancing out that agency and expertise and we do see this happening in emerging economies and developing countries where there is a greater sense of agency, a greater sense even of ownership of the essential principles of the TRIPS Agreement and an ability to adapt them to domestic needs, domestic priorities in a way that is better adapted to domestic circumstances and needs rather than seeing IP legislation as a kind of legislative to do list that’s been
set up by others. And by the same token we need to get away from the idea of the TRIPS Agreement as a kind of a model law as supplanting or displacing the domestic policy maker, the domestic legislator but rather providing a broad framework of adaptable and applicable principles that do and should move with the times, respond to technological change, to social change, to commercial change, to economic change, to cultural change and even in the jurisprudence we have concerning Article 13, the copyright exception to the three-step test, there is a reminder there that these tests are not fixed in time rooted to January 1, 1995 but rather do and should evolve over time and be applied in different ways with each new technological change. So it gets to actually how you apply them in practice rather than how we construe them in the abstract.

session_title: Super Session: Back to First Principles - Is the IP System Fit for the Age of AI?
speaker: Mr. Gaétan de Rassenfosse
affiliation: Associate Professor of Science Technology and Innovation Policy, Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Belgium
text:
Thank you very much for that question. I’m very happy you picked Fritz Meschlup’s quote because it really explains well economists’ ambivalence towards the IP system, sometimes too strong, sometimes too weak, but for sure imperfect. But to answer your question, so should we create in light of GNI a patent system as it is today? Well, the answer is no, but maybe not for the reason you expect. The reason is today’s system fundamentally doesn’t really work well.
So we don’t want that even in a non-AI world. And I’m thinking here more about patents. And the reason I’m saying that, well, we know it’s too slow. We know it’s too fragmented. We know the examination process is prone to error.
Sometimes it’s too powerful. Sometimes it’s too weak. So the system as we have it today is already not very well functioning. It’s functioning good enough, don’t get me wrong, but for sure we don’t want to create a new system from scratch that looks the same as we have today. But that begs then two following questions.
Well, what should the system look like to be GNI ready? And here I’m not talking in like five years but maybe like two years ago how it should have the system changed already. And another question is what will the actual system look like? And, of course, the answer to the two questions could differ. On the second question, what I believe will the system look like, well, my hunch it’s going to be very, very similar to what we have today.
Not much and I would be very happy to be proven wrong. But maybe we will have corporate inventorship for patents. Maybe we will have some tweaks on copyright law. But my hunch is the system as we have today would be very similar to the one we have tomorrow. Now what should in first best principle the system look like?
Well, that’s the more ambitious question obviously which we’re here to debate over the next couple of days. And I don’t have a final answer to that question but I just want to bring one thought to the room which is let’s go back to the very first patent system, the Venice patent statute of 1474, I think. So in the city of Venice, Italy where the system was actually conceived not necessarily to create inventions or to incentivize the creation of invention by local but particularly to attract invention from foreign craftsmen, to bring trademanship and craftsmanship to the city of Venice. And so very early on in the Venice patent statute, there was actually the willingness to attract foreign knowledge and diffuse technology. I think when we look at the situation today, especially in Gen AI or AI capabilities, while we see a very fragmented world, Europe is worried and rightly so to be lagging behind the U.S. in development and China in adoption.
And that’s not even mentioning Latin America, Africa, Southeast Asia. So if there is one feature that today’s IP system should actually encourage, it’s the development of indigenous innovation or the adoption of innovation in terms of AI in countries. I’ll stop here.

So I will briefly react on the verification and then I will go back to the incentive to innovate. And the point I want to spend time on the verification is we used to believe like a year or two years ago that verification would be the task that human would actually end up doing. So AI generates and then human verify. But more and more realize well, actually AI is pretty good at verifying too. And so we are having this discussion in the in a very dynamic and evolving landscape.
And so that’s why I don’t want to comment on that point specifically. But if you go back to the rationale on the incentive to invest or to invent, we should really wonder as a society what do we actually want as a first base, the social welfare? Do we want a world we have only machine innovating? Do we want a world where only human innovating or do you want a world where both collaborate or coexist? They might not collaborate, but they may coexist.
And if we have so I’m talking here in terms of the volume of economic activity that’s being created by humans or AI, right? Is it like 20/80, 80/20, 50/50? We don’t know. But actually this is very fundamental to how we should think about a revamped IP system knowing that the current IP system already affects that balance because it’s more or less favorable to different type of creators, AI versus I mean, machines versus humans. So we should really ask ourselves how do we want it to look like and be aware of the distinction.
But in addition to that, so we should, you know, given this, we should actually set up a system that essentially allows both modes of creation to flourish. And we should device a system that makes sure that we do not affect the direction of innovation, you know, departing from the way we want it. And let me give you a very concrete example to illustrate. Let’s assume we are at the beginning of a pandemic. And now a pharma company has a choice between hiring 20 data scientists and, you know, coming up with a new vaccine in three months or hiring 100 pharmacologists and coming up with a vaccine in a year.
You know, we don’t want the firm to take the decision based on the type of IP rights that it will get at the end. And so that’s when I say when we don’t want IP rights to bias what we want to be desirable as a society, this is precisely the point. So we will need an incentive to invest, you know, to invent in a way that is compatible to our social value. It might depend on fields, of course, you know, hardcore inventions versus creative industry, for instance.

I mean, to be honest in the first question, what is the role of IP in that concentration of power, I think it is IP’s secondary importance because there are so many things that matter so much more like the quality of human capital, the quality, I mean, the amount of VC investment, you know, a local cluster of innovation in Silicon Valley or China versus elsewhere. But now can we learn something indeed from standard essential patents, patent pools in terms of, you know, licensing agreements across essentially producers and users or implementers of technologies? I think we can. But I think but in two ways. So we know that things that work in terms of front terms but we also know that, let’s say, front terms are very vaguely defined and so that creates a lot of frictions in litigation eventually.
And so at the end of the day, you know, you solve a problem and you create another. Likewise for patent pools, patent pools allow the coordination of actors by pulling their IP and their specific regimes but at the same time there are players outside of patent pools that then start having disproportionate power and that creates another set of frictions. So we can learn a lot from this. The main difference that I see is between implementers, I mean, between the standard essential patents and, let’s say, the creative industry or, I mean, it’s books and copyrights and it’s essentially the fragmentation of actors. So we have a huge fragmentation of actors, both user and implementers or end users as opposed to SCPs where the ecosystem is fairly well defined.
And so I think that fragmentation will actually be a huge problem for coordination. There will be a lot of free riding around the central ecosystem which may defeat the purpose of coordination.

session_title: Super Session: Back to First Principles - Is the IP System Fit for the Age of AI?
speaker: Ms. Myrtha Hurtado Rivas
text:
Thank you so much, Stanley, for the question. I’ll try to speak slower. First of all, I’d like to clarify that I’m here in my personal capacity and not speaking on behalf of the company that employs me. The question is you ask about incentive, investment, trust, quality and origin, and I would say all of the above. Sometimes all of them combined.
Sometimes some of them isolated. But I think at least in business what we see is really a combination and actually an interconnection of those rights. When it comes to AI, I would say what I am observing is that the principles, the underlying principles of the IP system actually gets strengthened by AI. What is more difficult is how to maintain clarity and transparency on authenticity, origin, provenance, right? But on the other hand, because of AI, we see how important it is to strengthen the underlying principles.
What I like to kind of go towards is instead of us thinking about which is the most appropriate right to protect something, it’s much more the question which I try to raise with my business as well is to identify where is the value. And the value might not necessarily be in one single aspect. It goes back to the idea of mechanism and interplay. And this is nothing new for IP. But I think what AI brings is the additional element of data.
And I’m not here to say that we need a new right because not everything that has a value needs to be protected by IP. There is other ways we can achieve that. But I think it’s really important to look at this as a combination and interconnected elements achieving actually what we want, which is continued investment, innovation, creativity and access and so on. So I’ll pause here.

Thanks, Stanley. I’m going to try to be as short as possible looking at the time. My answer would be not necessarily. I don’t think that the fact that AI cuts down certain processes and accelerates certain developments in the development of pharmaceutical products will make it obsolete to have a patent term of a specific time frame. And I think one must differentiate the legal protection duration from the useful commercial life.
Those things have to come together. And I think to go back to the example of Professor Gaetan, when it is about this decision to be made, right, between what is it you do, hire 20 scientists or use AI to go faster, I think that’s where the balance comes in. Because you also need to consider how long actually this will be commercially viable. And I think, yes, there is an acceleration, but I don’t think that the patent term that we have today necessarily asks for a review of the same because the market will actually balance that out on itself. So I’ll keep it there just for sake of time.

But for how long have we talked about big data in pharma? When I was still working at the pharma originator business almost 15 years ago, it is when we started talking about big data. And then we realized even though we have centuries of data available, we realized the data couldn’t speak to each other. So then we realized, okay, probably it is not five years that we need until we can do something with this data. We probably need 15 years.
And even though today we have AI that helps us for the harmonization of data, well, we still are not there where we thought we would be 15 years ago. So yes, AI will accelerate a lot of things. We still need scientists and very bright human minds to connect the things, to evaluate, assess, and make the right judgment.

I think this goes back to a very simple lens. As a company, you will look as to where you will get the biggest aggregated return of investment. And you will need to make an assessment again as to how long your innovation will commercially be useful. That needs to be assessed case by case and it may be that you you end up with a combination of patent rights, trade secrets in certain countries by geographical scope, by product, by service, by launch time. All of that needs to be assessed together.
So I think today already we see that what we do is we use the mechanisms of the IP system and combine that with the other tools that we have at our hands which is licensing, contracts, data overall as the best way and I think it is not about it is about shifting the lens, not what is the right but rather where is the value and then use the best tools to protect that value.

session_title: Super Session: Back to First Principles - Is the IP System Fit for the Age of AI?
speaker: Ms. Chijioke Okorie
affiliation: Associate Professor of Law, University of Pretoria, Nigeria
text:
Thank you, Stanley. I think that the principles, the first principles on their own do not sufficiently justify IP system for Africa, at least not yet. And AI widens that gap but it also hands us an opportunity. The first principles rest mainly on the idea that individual exclusivity, when you give an individual exclusivity, you give the exclusive rights, the market will pay them back and they would create more and all of that. And the public interest will just only show up at the edges as exceptions.
But many African scholars, African creators and also users of IP protected materials have pushed back on that individualistic model. And so you and there are various reasons for that. One of the key reasons that you would find broadly in the literature is that the individualistic model of giving maybe an individual or a corporate body exclusivity would is problematic for African creators because they are a lot more collaborative, communal in the way that we create. And you find that example in various sectors across Africa. There is a lot more people building as communities and it is difficult to find or to be able to say that this one person is responsible for creating or inventing this.
So you look at how exceptions have played out in relation to Africa and the rest of the world. You find that with patents, for example, African countries have pushed for exceptions, especially so that they can have access to affordable medicines and also pushed for exceptions so that there is a drive against evergreening in the pharmaceutical sector. But in copyright, you find that exceptions are not so popular for creators because they really want to identify with that exclusivity just so that there is that exchange where the market pays them back. But when you look at AI, you find that exceptions are quite popular with AI developers and you would have heard strings of that from what Cedric said. So there is all that tension.
But it is the same tool, the same IP tool, but there is also the same word "access" where you are now looking at the question is now access for who and who is going to pay for the investment in the creative process in the inventive and innovative processes. So you take Nollywood, for example, because why wouldn’t I mention Nollywood? I am Nigerian. Around more than two thousand films a year.
The budget is low. Piracy is significant. But it is not necessarily exclusivity that builds that industry. It is more creators coming together, collaborating, giving whatever they have to make sure that we come up with something. But when the real money comes up, you find that it comes from global platforms.
So you see if you are a If you are a film lover, you would find that there is a lot of movies that are being released from Nigeria on YouTube and Cedric, there is a lot of money coming from YouTube, from Google to those creators. But the point I am trying to make is that there is always the reason why those principles haven’t served as much and the reasons reason why I say that AI provides us with an opportunity is that there is money coming from IP because you own these things, you are able to determine how they are distributed, how they are disseminated. So there is some connection with those principles existing. But the issue is that the payment is not necessarily coming from the very users themselves but are coming from other parties or other stakeholders who are part of the distribution chain but not part of the user system. So will the first principles continue to serve?
Not currently in the form that they exist. But instead it is more distributive justice, restorative justice which are the principles that African scholars have first have mostly put up as the appropriate justification for IP systems where creators get paid, inventors and innovators get remunerated, users have access to the work but in a way that everybody gets what they are supposed to get and in a way that the system is more balanced as opposed to insisting on exclusivity as the very thing that will give us payment or remuneration.

I think that the I want to pick up from where from the issue of collective, collectively created work because I did mention that there’s a lot more collective, collaborative, communal, you know, creative processes that happen across African societies. The thing with collective licensing in that sense is that in and of itself, collective licensing is not a problem. It’s not a risk. The risk lies in the governance of collective management organizations, collective licensing solutions themselves. If you look across the African continent, what you will find is that collective licensing has given us a better solution in terms of people being able to directly reach creators, directly reach inventors, directly reach innovators because now there’s more, there’s higher bargaining power for you to be able to negotiate as a collective to say this is what we want or this is what we don’t want.
Where things have gone wrong is in the governance, in the accountability, in the transparency of those organizations in how they handle revenue or monies being paid to them to now give over to their members. The second thing also is that collective societies have also not given themselves to, there’s need for more infrastructure in terms of resources that enable them to be better at metadata, be better at tagging, be better at managing the vast volume of creative and inventive data. Also remember that licensing cuts both ways. You are not just speaking of licensing already existing creative works, you are also We are also talking about AI solutions and AI tools that are also themselves possibly IP protected and we see a lot of that happening in the African continent where there is not just use of AI tools that are imported from outside the continent, but there are AI developers that are building AI solutions on the continent and that’s also possibly subject of licensing. Collective licensing would also be able to play a role in that space.
Finally, collective licensing is not just a copyright solution. We also see collective licensing in the patent space where it’s standard setting organizations and standard essential patents where now you have patent pools and people being able to license as a collective in that space. It’s the same solution, lower transaction cost, higher beginning power because now you have mass of inventors or creators. Where we need to solve is in the governance so that collective organizations or licensing organizations are transparent and accountable and have access to infrastructure and that’s where also technology can also play a role to make them better at their jobs.

speaker: Ms. Jennifer Tauli (Jing) Corpuz

Thank you very much, Stanley, for the question. If I were in court I would say the question is leading which makes it easy for me, actually. Moderator is provocative. But, I mean, this is exactly the reason why we have ongoing negotiations within the context of the IGC, right, to answer this question of whether we can adapt the conventional Intellectual Property system to also protect collectively generated knowledge and expressions. And I think we took a first small step forward with the GRTK Treaty which recognizes that, well, Genetic Resources are owned by group of people, by the nation, in some instances by Indigenous Peoples or local communities and that there is also traditional knowledge involved in some ways that Genetic Resources are discovered.
So it’s a small step in a way that for me transforms the foundation of the system to also recognize collective knowledge and I think it’s good that I’m coming after my seat mate here because indeed in many places, but especially in Indigenous Peoples’ contexts, the Intellectual Property system as it currently is does not protect the knowledge that we generate. But at the same time, it’s very clear that there is value because of the 6,000 languages, for example, all over the world, 5,000 are Indigenous Languages. And those languages correspond to cultures that are quite diverse and quite rich and a source of inspiration for creating creators. We see increasingly copying of Indigenous and local community generated designs, especially in the runways, right, of Paris, of New York and so forth, which means that there is value. And I think, you know, there should not be any difference between individual creators and collective creators because these are all creations that have beauty, that have intrinsic value and, you know, it’s been more than 20 years with the IGC, but I hope that we can still find the way forward to customizing the Intellectual Property system to protect collectively generated, transmitted, maintained knowledge and expressions.
Now, on the question of AI, I think it’s both it’s a double-edged sword. So it’s been used, there are many reflection sessions among different Indigenous Peoples’ groups now to see what how the tools can be used to benefit Indigenous Peoples, but also what the risks are. Okay. There are clear benefits, like in recovering dying languages, which is something that seems to be important because it’s now the international decade of Indigenous Languages. And there is however, there is also the other edge of the sword, a danger of further homogenizing Indigenous Peoples, stereotyping, strengthening the stereotypes of Indigenous Peoples, but also heightening the risk of misappropriation and misuse of traditional knowledge and traditional cultural expressions.
So there are many examples, but maybe we can cite them in the next round. So what are the first principles? Maybe I’ll end with this question. We need to have, as you said, the concept of free prior and informed consent in the center, but also what are the customary laws of Indigenous Peoples that guide how these different design elements and traditional knowledge elements can be used and can’t be used? Because as you said, there is a sacred element to a lot of this.
A very quick example from my community is designs that are meant for burials, right? For the dead, that were used in an inappropriate way and caused a lot of distress in the Philippines. So the Vice President used this fabric and this design in one of the state of the nation addresses. And of course, the people from the neighboring community where I’m from said that no, this is not appropriate. It’s used for burials, for burial blankets.
And so, you know, there is value in looking at what the customary rules are for uses of these different elements of knowledge and expressions.

Well, in a word, yes, it makes it more urgent. Many Indigenous Peoples have pointed out the perils of AI. And this is because as with the first question that you asked, right now, collectively created work is not protected under the IP system, right? So anything that has been documented from Indigenous Peoples that has been put on the Internet is basically not protected. And so it can be used in the current regime to train, you know, to train AI models without consent, right?
And so there but at the same time, because of the technological power that AI and the new technologies now have, we are also thinking of beyond the IGC, what could be technological approaches that would, you know, such as metadata, for example, the tagging that are used by local contexts, which is basically putting elements of culture online, but tagging them through the metadata with information about who you should get consent from, what are the rules for using that design, and how may you use it and how may you not use the design. So this is an open question, right? Is how do we use the power of the technology that is available now to tag certain elements of collective culture with the rules that apply to them. So this may be something that’s developed within the IGC context.
It may be developed independently. I think personally that the IIII that has been initiated by WIPO has great potential to look at these approaches, but the fact remains is that collective creators are like individual creators also. We create something that produces value and, therefore, we should be able to authorize and control the way that it’s used.

session_title: Insight: Painting by Numbers - The Power of IP Data
speaker: Mr. Garrett Levin
text:
Thank you. We have one more session before lunch and I will be brief but not fast. You are welcome, colleagues. When chatGPT burst onto the scene in late 2022, it seemed to many of us as though AI revolution had arrived almost out of nowhere. But had it really?
Back in 2019, WIPO’s technology trends report on artificial intelligence was already telling a rather different story. Scientific publications in AI had been growing rapidly for decades and patent applications were following a similarly dramatic trajectory with exponential growth in the years leading up to the report. The signals were there but the question was were we paying attention to them? And that raises a very interesting possibility. If patent and scientific data could have helped us anticipate the AI revolution, what might they be telling us about the next breakthrough, technology?
Our next insight, painting by numbers, the power of IP data explores how IP information can offer not just a record of past innovation but a window into its future. To help us connect the dots, please welcome to the stage Mr. Andrew Tool, associate professor of public policy at the Georgia Institute of Technology.

session_title: Insight: Painting by Numbers - The Power of IP Data
speaker: Mr. Andrew Toole
affiliation: Associate Professor of Public Policy, Georgia Institute of Technology, United States of America
text:
Good afternoon, everyone. And thank you to the organizers for this opportunity. I appreciate it very much. I think all of us here really understand the potential of new technologies to fundamentally change our daily lives, our job opportunities and even our interpersonal relationships. So let’s think about could we actually identify new technologies as they emerge?
If we can do that, we are going to change our perspective from being retrospective to prospective. That is to say when we have a prospective understanding, we have the opportunity to shape the ecosystem to provide the policies, the incentives and the infrastructure that will define and allow us to harness the benefits of the new technology. If we are proactive, we are also able to set up governance structures if those are necessary to protect people from the new technology. And, of course, if we are proactive, we can have our IP offices understand the staffing needs that they are going to need so that they can continue to have quality examination and low pendency. So the question is can IP data help us to be proactive by allowing us to identify emerging technologies early?
My answer is yes. So the patent data are indispensable source for identifying emerging technologies. However, they cannot be used in isolation. The key is detecting the language of discovery in science and in industry that will fuel early and follow on inventions. So to illustrate this point, I would like to go through the case of the emergence of generative AI and we first we know that it was probably an amazing eye opening experience in November of 2022 when chat GPT burst onto the scene.
It was and so the question is could we have anticipated the that bursting of chat GPT? Well, today we have the, you know, the power of hindsight, the 2020 vision that we can look back in time, we can see what actually happened and we can learn lessons from that information. So here is what the U.S. patent data were showing. Each bar counts the U.S. patent applications that named generative AI model, things like generative adversarial network, variational auto encoder or transformer. So for years, the count was near zero.
But it then in 2017 and 2018, it turns up. Twelve applications in 2017. 67 applications in 2018. Almost 200 applications in 2019. And nearly 600 by 2022.
So by the time chat GPT arrived, these filings had been rising for about five years, a half of a decade. So after chat GPT exploded or onto the scene, there were more than 4600 applications in 2025 for generative AI. So the signal was there and it was actually in plain sight. So let me put this on a timeline. The inventions behind the first rise were filed in 2016 and 2017.
And most patents have an 18-month period before they are made public. And so we see the rise publicly in 2018. Now look at what came next. In January 2019, as was just mentioned, WIPO published its technology trends report on artificial intelligence, an excellent report. The patent coverage of that report extended only to early of 2018.
Now WIPO names in that report deep learning, neural networks as the fastest growing AI techniques. But there is no mention of generative adversarial networks in that document. The key GAN, that’s the short, the key GAN paper was nearly four years old when the data were pulled for that report. Georgetown University followed up quickly on what WIPO had done, an excellent report in their center for security and emerging technology with a consulting company, 1790 analytics. They adapted and applied the WIPO definitions but their data ended in March of 2020.
And CHATGPT was launched in November of 2022. And just weeks after that, in January of 2023, both the IPC, the international patent classification and the CPC classification system added a code for generative AI. And WIPO published its landscape on generative AI in July of 2024. So the gold band in the graphic here represents nearly five years when the signal was public if we had known what to look for. And so why didn’t we see it?
Why didn’t we see it? Because we didn’t know the language that described and characterized the new technology. This picture shows the words used in US AI patent applications published in 2018 and 2019. The bigger the word, the more applications used it. In those years, AI meant things like recognizing images, speech, faces, vehicles, even robots.
The gold words on the graphic are the language of generative AI. So generative and language model each appear about one in 200 AI applications at that time compared with image which appeared in one out of every four AI application at that time. Which raises the question where could we have learned about the language of generative AI so that we could actually trace the emergence of this technology? So the answer is science. And to some extent industry.
The language of a new technology appears in research before it appears in inventions. And this diagram, the Sandkey diagram shows that flow. On the left are the words inventors used to name their generative AI models. Each family of words was coined in research papers and the labels show which paper and when. On the right are the U.S. Patent applications published from 2018 to 2022, that five-year window before CHAT GPT.
The width of each band is a count of patent applications. So almost four in five of these applications used language coined in research in 2013 and 2014. Auto encoders, word embeddings, sequence to sequence models and above all generative adversarial networks which alone accounted for 860 of the 1726 applications. Now look at the bottom of this graphic, the language of the next wave of generative AI. Pretrained language models, diffusion models, those were coined in research in 2018 and through 2020 and it’s already there in a very thin line, only 37 applications at that time.
So the words of the CHAT GPT era were in the patent record even before CHAT GPT. They were just really small. So in principle we could see them if we knew what we were looking for. So the trip from science to invention actually goes quickly. It’s surprising actually how fast it happens.
Patents cite the research they build on. Each gray dot in this graphic is a landmark research paper. The gold dots are the U.S. patents that cite it, placed at the year the application was filed. The bigger the dot, the more patents. The first GAN paper was published in 2014 and inventors cited it in applications filed in 2015.
57 applications were filed in 2017. The transformer paper published in June of 2017 was cited in applications that very same year. The GPT3 and the diffusion model both from 2020 were cited in filings from 2020. In other words, inventors were building on these breakthroughs within a year or two. And the path from science to patents is fast and it’s measurable.
So this is a short presentation because we’re going to lunch and I don’t want to delay anything. But that’s the brief case study of generative AI. Now let’s put it all back together. And if you do this, if you step back from generative AI and put these signals in order, we get a ladder. Each rung comes earlier than the one above it.
At the top we have the new classification codes from the patent offices in January 2023. Below it, the market breakthrough, the moment everybody notices the chat GPT in November 2022. Below that, new words published in patent applications visible in 2018. Then patents citing new science as early as 2015. And at the bottom, the very kind of root research clusters that grow fast, GAN papers went from 68 in 2016 to almost 600 in 2017.
And Georgetown University in near Washington, D.C., they have a center for security and emerging technology that I’m associated with. That’s why I know about this. They’re building maps of science, of research clusters, the language of research. And they’re connecting the language of research to the language of patent applications. And that’s exactly the lowest rung on this ladder.
And that’s where the roots of the new technology come from. So back to the question, can IP data help us to be proactive? And the answer is yes. Patent data are an indispensable source of identifying emerging technologies. But they cannot be viewed in isolation.
The key, again, is detecting the language and discovery of science in this discovery of science in industry and taking that language to the patent data. If we do that, we can have a proactive stance as policymakers and as citizens. We are able to more readily shape the ecosystems that these technologies are coming into, set up our governance structures if needed, and, of course, help our IP offices to do a great job. Thank you. Yeah, thank you.
